blocks.text: Yet one objection can be raised, namely that the Hebrew הבנים hobnim is a plural, whereas the word for ebony is only singular. It is indeed inflected and spelled in various ways. For one says haec ebenus, or evenus, or hebenus, and hoc ebenum, or evenum, [II, 718] or hebenum. And in Greek ἡ ἔβενος [hē ebenos], or ἔβελος [ebelos], as in the Suda; or ἐβένη [ebenē], as in Theophrastus. But in the plural, ἐβένους [ebenous] in Greek was said only by Symmachus; and in Latin ebenos or ebena only, as far as I remember, by Arias and Mercerus in their rendering of this passage. Junius answers that it is named in the plural by the Hebrews because there are two kinds of ebony. That is indeed what Theophrastus teaches, Hist. book 4, ch. 5, where he treats the trees of India: Ἴδιον δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐβένη τῆς χώρας ταύτης. Ταύτης δὲ δύο γένη τὸ μὲν εὔξυλον, καὶ καλόν· τὸ δὲ φαῦλον. σπάνιον δὲ τὸ καλὸν, θάτερον δὲ πολύ. Τὴν δὲ χρόαν οὐ θησαυριζομένη λαμβάνει τὴν εὔχρουν, ἀλλ᾽ εὐθὺς τῇ φύσει ἐστὶ δὲ τὸ δένδρον θαμνῶδες, ὥσπερ ὁ κύτισος [Idion de kai hē ebenē tēs chōras tautēs. Tautēs de dyo genē to men euxylon, kai kalon; to de phaulon. spanion de to kalon, thateron de poly. Tēn de chroan ou thēsaurizomenē lambanei tēn euchroun, all᾽ euthys tē physei estin de to dendron thamnōdes, hōsper ho kytisos]. Ebony too is peculiar to this region. Of it there are two kinds: one of excellent wood, and good; the other bad. The good one is rare, but the other common. Nor does ebony acquire its fine colour by being stored away, but has it at once from nature. Moreover it is like a shrub, as the cytisus is. That this is the true meaning of Theophrastus Salmasius proves at length in his Exercitations on Solinus, and not the one that Pliny, book 12, chapter 4, ascribes to him in these words: There are two kinds of it. The rarer is the better one, tree-like, with a trunk [col. 143] free of knots, its wood of a black lustre, and pleasing at once even without craftsmanship. The other is shrubby, like the cytisus, and spread over all India. Good ebony is not called εὔξυλος [euxylos] because it is tree-like, that is, large like a tree, but from the excellence of its wood. Nor is being θαμνώδης [thamnōdēs] peculiar to the bad kind; it is common to both. And there θαμνῶδες [thamnōdes] does not mean fruticosum [shrubby], that is, dense with many twigs, but behaving like a shrub, as all bushes do. Dioscorides also makes two kinds of ebony, but distinguishes them by place: Ἔβενος κρατίστη ἡ Αἰθιοπικὴ, καὶ μέλαινα, καὶ μὴ ἔχουσα κτηδόνας [Ebenos kratistē hē Aithiopikē, kai melaina, kai mē echousa ktēdonas]; The best ebony is the Ethiopian, black, and without veins running through it like the teeth of a comb. The Arabic translator calls them طبقات [ṭabaqāt]. And a little later: Ἔστι δέ τις καὶ Ἰνδικὴ, ἔχουσα διαφύσεις λευκὰς, καὶ κιῤῥὰς, καὶ σπίλους ὁμοίως πυκνούς· πλὴν βελτίων ἡ πρώτη [Esti de tis kai Indikē, echousa diaphyseis leukas, kai kirrhas, kai spilous homoiōs pyknous; plēn beltiōn hē prōtē]. There is also another, Indian, with white and reddish lines running through it, and frequent spots as well. But the former is better. So also Isidore: Ebony grows in India and Ethiopia; when cut it hardens into stone; its wood is black, and its bark smooth like that of the laurel. But the Indian is spotted, with small white and tawny markings. The Ethiopian, however, which is held to be superior, is spotted nowhere, but black, smooth and horn-like. And Serapion: It has two species, namely Absi and Inda. And Absi is a black wood, without lines, etc. In the Indian, however, there are white lines, and of a reddish colour, etc. This is taken from Dioscorides. Absi is حبشي [ḥabashī] Habasi, that is, Ethiopian. Common to all of these is that they recognize only two species of ebony. To which the Hebrew הבנים hobnim does not correspond, because it is a plural, not a dual noun. For the dual would be hobnajim. So something else must be sought. Fuller indeed refers this plural to the palangae of ebony, which were brought from India and Ethiopia in great [II, 719] numbers. Herodotus and Arrian in the Periplus call them φάλαγγας [phalangas]; Pliny palangae or phalangae, the spelling varying; that is, round poles, such as are placed under ships, or on which several men carry the same load. Pollux, book 7, ch. 33, §. 9: Τὰ δὲ τῶν νεῶν ξύλα, οἷς ὑποβληθεῖσιν ἐφέλκονται αἱ νῆες, φάλαγγες, καὶ φαλάγγια [Ta de tōn neōn xyla, hois hypoblētheisin ephelkontai hai nēes, phalanges, kai phalangia]. Hesychius: Φαλάγγια· στρόγγυλα ξύλα, καὶ σύμμετρα [Phalangia; strongyla xyla, kai symmetra]. Nonius: Palangae is the name for round poles which are put under ships when they are drawn down to the sea, or when they are hauled up onto the shore. The Glosses: Phalangarii, Οἱ τοῖς δοκοῖς ἀποκρεμῶντες βάρη, καὶ πλείονες ἅμα βαστάζοντες [Hoi tois dokois apokremōntes barē, kai pleiones hama bastazontes]. Again Nonius: We call palangarii those who carry some load on poles. The origin of the word seems to be Hebrew. For in Hebrew פלך pelec, or in archaic form phelec, is baculus [staff], 2 Sam. III, 29. And in Arabic فلك [falaka] phalaca means to be round. Hence the round ebony staves which the Tyrian merchants called פלכין pelakin or phelakin could have been called φάλαγγες [phalanges], phalanges, or palanges. Callixenus, in book 5 of Athenaeus, names ἐβένου κορμοὺς [ebenou kormous], logs of ebony. Apuleius, in the first Apology, staves of ebony, though some prefer to read loculos [little boxes] there. These, then, whether staves or κορμοὺς [kormous], or these palangae of ebony, Fuller thinks are signified by the plural הבנים hobnim. But learned men seem to weary themselves here in vain, since the Hebrews scarcely name precious woods of this kind otherwise than with a plural word. Thus the tree from which the ark was made is called once in the singular שטה sitta, Es. XLI, 19. But in the plural שטים sittim more than twenty times in Exodus. And another tree, from which the beams and supports in the temple of Solomon were made, and the harps and lutes of the singers, is called only by a plural word, אלגומים algumim or אלמוגים almugim, 1 Reg. X, 11. 12. and 2 Par. IX, 10. 11. And in the Chaldee paraphrases of Jonathan and Jerusalem, Gen. L, 1: Joseph laid his father בערס דסנדפין, on a couch of sindaphin, that is, as they hold, on a bed made of the most excellent kind of wood, so called with a plural word. [col. 144] And I once suspected that it was so named after two villages of Egypt called سندف [Sndf] Sendapha. Yet in the treatise On the Elephant above, a truer explanation of this word is given.
